strengths: The manuscript addresses a relevant problem: predicting human response times under changing environmental cues. Combining task-trained representations, human-response prediction, and an accumulation-based adjustment is a plausible and potentially useful modeling contribution. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-01/reviews/b07/review-experiment-0cm4swbr/call-4c685bb987c34563aed33af09d846873/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The two-day study provides a substantial collection of 21,157 responses across four pressure conditions, with 36 participants retained after exclusions. Collecting choices, response times, and subjective attention/anxiety ratings creates a useful empirical resource. Public data and code links are provided.

Evaluation covers pooled, group-specific, individual-specific, and leave-one-participant-out settings. The hybrid model reports lower overall MAPE than pure DRL in all four settings, including 0.3037 to 0.2905 under participant holdout. The representation comparison also supports the usefulness of task-trained features, and the reported training-time reduction is practically encouraging.
weaknesses: The central claim of explaining the underlying cognitive process is insufficiently supported. The Methods section constructs a sigmoid trajectory from SVM-predicted response time and choice probability, without specifying a stochastic diffusion process or validating the correspondence to DDM parameters. Terminal response-time supervision cannot uniquely identify the intermediate action trajectory: many trajectories can produce the same boundary-crossing time. Consequently, visualizing these trajectories and recovering aggregate response-time trends does not establish that they represent human evidence accumulation or adaptation.

The evaluation does not isolate the value of modeling stimuli at fine temporal resolution. Pressure trials use the same repeating five-second progress bar, but there are no comparisons against a pressure indicator plus elapsed-time features, shuffled frames, or removal of visual inputs. Figure 7 also shows substantial inferred 'time pressure effects' in the no-pressure group. This suggests that the learned actions can correct ordinary SVM prediction errors, making their interpretation as stimulus effects questionable.

The baselines do not establish which component produces the gains. Pure DRL uses concatenated Inception-V3 video features, whereas hybrid DRL processes individual frames with a different encoder; action parameterizations and episode structures also differ. These differences confound both accuracy and training-efficiency comparisons. Strong supervised response-time predictors with pressure/history covariates and established accumulation models are missing. Although related RL–DDM work is cited, the distinctive benefit over existing approaches remains inadequately demonstrated.

The predictive improvements need uncertainty estimates. Relative MAPE reductions over pure DRL range from approximately 1.2% to 4.3%, but confidence intervals for the differences, repeated-run variability, and participant-level paired comparisons are not reported. The participant dots in Figure 6 show heterogeneity rather than uncertainty in the improvement. Shuffled trial splits and selected chronological examples also provide limited evidence for forecasting future behavior; a chronological holdout would strengthen that claim.

The training protocol leaves consequential ambiguities. It is unclear which observations train the purported no-pressure SVM baseline and whether every human-supervised stage is refitted within each evaluation fold, including participant holdout. Thus, independence of the complete prediction pipeline cannot be verified from the manuscript. Essential implementation details are also missing, including the sigmoid parameterization, the value of the perturbation factor λ, and numerical thresholds for the adaptive feedback rule.

The human-study conclusions require more careful statistical support. Retained groups contain only 7–10 participants, and the criterion for excluding three participants as extreme outliers is unspecified. Handling of the ten-second response-time cap is also unclear. The stated use of paired post hoc t-tests between independently assigned groups requires clarification or correction. Furthermore, nonsignificant accuracy effects do not establish equivalence, so they only weakly justify treating accuracy as unaffected by pressure.

Smaller reporting inconsistencies should be corrected. Figure 4(a) appears to contain 4,067 correct predictions out of 4,083, approximately 99.61%, rather than the stated 99.93%. The terminal-state description also uses R_t for an evidence boundary elsewhere denoted R_p. These are secondary to the validation concerns, but they reduce confidence in the technical presentation.
